analysis.one_liner: Bans mid-decade congressional redistricting and forbids maps drawn to favor any political party.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the final two weeks of the 117th Congress with no cosponsors, the bill died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set nationwide rules for how states draw congressional districts: each state gets one map per decade, with mid-decade redraws banned unless a court requires one. Maps could not be drawn with the intent or effect of materially favoring either political party, and they would have to protect minority voting rights and keep communities together. States would have to run an open process with public map-drawing tools and hearings, and if a state missed a deadline or drew an illegal map, a federal court would take over and draw the map itself. Because the Supreme Court has said federal courts will not police partisan gerrymandering, only Congress can set these rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters in heavily gerrymandered states, whose votes are currently diluted when maps are drawn to guarantee one party's wins. Communities of interest that get split across districts, and minority voters whose ability to elect candidates of choice would be explicitly protected. Citizens, who would gain access to public map-drawing software, hearings, and posted data instead of back-room map deals.

how_it_helps.text: States could not redraw congressional maps more than once per decade unless a court orders it, ending repeat mid-cycle redraws that shift district lines between elections.

A map could not be used if, viewed statewide, it was drawn with the intent or has the effect of materially favoring or disfavoring any political party, measured by statistical tests of partisan fairness against recent election results.

Districts must comply with the Voting Rights Act, including creating districts where protected groups can elect representatives of choice, and must respect communities of interest and neighborhoods where practicable.

Map-drawing bodies would have to hold hearings around the state, post all proposed maps and data on a public website with free map-drawing software, and publish a written evaluation of each plan before voting.
The Attorney General or any aggrieved citizen could sue over a noncompliant map; a court finding a violation would adopt a replacement plan rather than leave the illegal map in place.

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent members of Congress and the state politicians who draw their districts would lose the power to entrench themselves with party-favoring maps, and states would bear the cost of an open, documented map-drawing process. If a state failed to comply, a federal court would take over its mapmaking.
analysis.who_pays_short: Incumbent lawmakers who draw their own maps

drawbacks.text: States whose existing maps do not comply would have to enact a new, compliant plan within 45 days of the bill becoming law, forcing a rushed nationwide round of redistricting outside the normal once-a-decade cycle.
If a state missed the deadline, a federal three-judge court — not any elected body — would take over and draw the state's congressional map, moving mapmaking from elected officials to judges.

The bill's partisan-fairness test relies on statistical measures such as the efficiency gap, which voting scholars have criticized as a rough proxy that can flag plans in closely divided states while missing severe distortions elsewhere, so the enforcement standard could misfire in both directions.

The bill covers only congressional districts, not the state legislative districts that determine who governs states, and it awards no monetary damages to people who win lawsuits over gerrymandered maps.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill — one map per decade, no party-favoring maps, an open public process — addresses a real problem that the Supreme Court has declined to fix, and the 7% partisan-advantage threshold is forgiving enough to leave closely balanced states alone. The honest costs are real: the 45-day compliance deadline would force a rushed round of mapmaking, and court-drawn maps replace one unelected process (partisan map deals) with another (judicial drawing). The bill's strength is that it applies the same rules to both parties' maps and to maps already in effect, rather than only to future ones.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 21, 2022, two weeks before the Congress ended, referred to the Judiciary Committee, and died there without a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Senator Klobuchar introduced the bill on December 21, 2022, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
No other action was ever taken on the bill; it received no committee hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
No senator joined as a cosponsor; the bill's support was limited to its single Democratic sponsor.
Under the bill's terms, even maps already in effect would have had to comply, so enactment would have required states to re-enact their 2021 maps to meet the new criteria within 45 days.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lawmakers and state parties that drew their 2021 congressional maps to their own advantage keep those maps untouched and retain the power to redraw districts whenever they choose, with no federal rule constraining them.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Redistricting Reform Act of 2022 on December 21, 2022.

against.name: Sen. Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup during the final two weeks of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no Republican signed on, so no partisan split was ever tested; the bill ended with one Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party.

industries.industry: Incumbent House members and the state politicians who draw congressional maps
industries.note: These officeholders currently control where their own district lines fall and use that power to guarantee their party's seats. The bill would strip that power, banning mid-decade redraws and maps that materially favor either party, and applies to maps already in effect.

industries.industry: State political parties with gerrymandering operations
industries.note: Parties that invested in computer-assisted map drawing to lock in seat advantages would lose that edge, and any registered voter could sue over a party-favoring map. Their gain from favorable maps comes directly at the cost of other voters' representation.
